title: Lamps Left On After Every Round
statement:
A hallway has n lamps numbered 1 to n, all switched off. You make n rounds. In round k you flip the switch of every lamp whose number is a multiple of k: on becomes off, off becomes on.

So round 1 turns every lamp on, round 2 flips lamps 2, 4, 6, …, round 3 flips 3, 6, 9, …, and the last round flips only lamp n.

Return how many lamps are on after all n rounds.

examples.why: After round 1: all on. Round 2 turns lamp 2 off. Round 3 turns lamp 3 off. Only lamp 1 stays on.
Lamps 1, 4 and 9 end up on. Lamp 6 is flipped in rounds 1, 2, 3 and 6, an even number of times, so it ends off.

hints: Follow one lamp, say lamp 12. In which rounds is it flipped?
Lamp i is flipped once for every divisor of i. It ends on exactly when it has an odd number of divisors.
Divisors come in pairs d and i / d. A pair collapses into one divisor only when d = i / d, that is when i is a perfect square. Count the squares up to n.

explain.intuition:
Stop simulating rounds and look at one lamp. Lamp i is flipped in round k exactly when k divides i, so the number of flips is the number of divisors of i. It starts off, so it ends on only if that number is odd.

Divisors pair up: 12 has (1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4), an even count. The only way to get an odd count is a divisor paired with itself, d · d = i. So exactly the perfect squares stay on, and the answer is the number of squares in 1..n, which is ⌊√n⌋.
steps: Note that lamp i is flipped once per divisor of i.
Odd number of divisors ⇔ i is a perfect square.
Count the squares 1, 4, 9, … up to n: that is ⌊√n⌋.
Compute it with Math.sqrt and correct by ±1 if floating point rounded across a square.
pitfalls: Simulating the rounds. That is about n log n flips, far too many for n = 10⁹.
Trusting a floating square root blindly in languages with less precise math. Checking k · k ≤ n after rounding removes any doubt.
Thinking primes matter. Lamp 6 is not prime and lamp 4 is not prime, but only one of them stays on.

solutions.title: Simulate every round
solutions.idea: Keep a boolean per lamp and flip multiples of k for every round k.

solutions.title: Count perfect squares
solutions.idea: Only lamps with an odd number of divisors stay on, and those are the perfect squares. There are ⌊√n⌋ of them.
